name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau, 13.7% of firms in the religious organisations category (NAICS 81) reported using AI in the two weeks prior to survey, up from 12.6% in the prior period. This official measure, though modest, reflects early-stage adoption across the hundreds of thousands of congregations and faith organisations operating in the United States. The sourced points note that Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series, making it the most reliable baseline available, though no deeper sectoral breakdown currently exists.

The sources point toward a landscape where faith organisations are beginning to explore AI for ministry and operations, but the sector's posture remains cautious and values-driven. Gloo, a technology platform serving thousands of US churches, frames its offering around values-aligned AI models and developer tools designed specifically for faith-based missions, suggesting that congregations seeking to adopt AI are doing so with explicit concern for alignment between the technology and their theological commitments. The platform emphasises inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows tailored to ministry contexts, pointing toward practical applications in knowledge management and decision-making rather than autonomous or high-stakes processes.

Ethical questions dominate the sector's engagement with AI adoption. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit network, positions itself to bring time-tested faith-based values and wisdom to the ethical AI conversation, noting that for 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation, AI's emerging issues around control, power, privacy, bias and discrimination, economic well-being, and human meaning are deeply spiritual as well. Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good hosts research and convenings—including a DELTA summit centring human formation and dignity in the AI transition—reflecting institutional concern that AI deployment in faith contexts must grapple with labour displacement and what meaningful work and human flourishing look like when technology can perform tasks faster and cheaper.

Barna Group, the Christian research organisation tracking trends affecting faith, culture and ministry, and the Hartford Institute for Religion Research, which has 45 years of history surveying congregational life, appear to be the primary sources monitoring adoption, perception, and use patterns among US congregations and ministry leaders. The sources, however, do not yet provide published findings on specific deployment outcomes, return on investment, or measurable pastoral or operational gains from AI use in congregations. Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life programme periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology, though the excerpts provided do not detail their specific AI findings.

What emerges is a sector at an early adoption phase, characterised by both pragmatic interest in AI tooling for administration and ministry and a deep institutional emphasis on values alignment and ethical governance. Faith organisations appear to be approaching AI adoption with more caution and moral deliberation than some other sectors, driven by the conviction that AI's alignment with human dignity, theological values, and worker wellbeing matters intrinsically, not merely instrumentally. A congregation or faith leader considering AI deployment should expect to engage both technical capability and ethical framework, and to draw on resources like Gloo's values-alignment measures, AI and Faith's ethical convening work, and the broader scholarly output from Notre Dame and other faith-based research institutions.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community to tackle pressing ethical issues. It promotes interdisciplinary research, policy leadership, and practical models for ethical AI design, development, and deployment. The institute will host a second DELTA summit focused on human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Sullivan notes that many industry workers “talk very flippantly” about job displacement and AI’s speed and cost, while Lily Abadal observes that AI awareness is evolving.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: Gloo AI offers faith-based and missional organizations a suite of trusted, values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks to help build AI that reflects their values. The platform provides an API-first system for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, along with a connected infrastructure of production tools, trusted content, and models. Gloo AI reports the first comprehensive evaluation framework that measures AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. It also supplies knowledge-graph integration, secure infrastructure, and specialized agents that coordinate workflows and power mission-specific solutions, with expert teams designing custom models and infrastructure for missional organizations.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
